newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rexrodt sees turnaround in German labour market.
newsitem.headline: Rexrodt sees turnaround in German labour market.

text.p: Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Tuesday the record unemployment that led Germany to raise its 1997 deficit forecast will ease in spring, leaving it in line to qualify for European monetary union.

Briefing journalists on the government's annual report on the economy, Rexrodt said severe winter weather had again boosted joblessness, raising the deficit by cutting tax revenues and forcing up outlays for benefits.

The official outlook now sees a total government budget deficit of 105 billion marks, or 2.9 percent of gross domestic product, up from an earlier 2.5 percent, and precariously close to the three percent level required to qualify for EMU.
Average unemployment in 1997 should be about 200,000 higher than last year's 3.9 million, but a turnaround starting in April or May will create new jobs, Rexrodt said.
Each additional 100,000 unemployed costs the government four billion to five billion marks, he said.

Unemployment in December rose to 4.15 million, and some officials have forecast it will peak at a post-war record 4.5 million this year. Rexrodt said, however, he believes that by year-end unemployment will be below the December level.
A rebound in economic growth to 2.5 percent this year from 1.4 percent in 1996 will propel the turnaround, he said.
"I believe we will not miss the criteria" for EMU, he said. But he also indicated some doubts about his own optimistic scenario.
"We will reach our goals only with a committed continuation of the reform measures we have begun," Rexrodt said.
"Unfortunately, the awareness of the need for such reforms is not yet sufficiently developed. Reforms are unpopular because they threaten vested interests."

The government has met great scepticism with its Programme for More Jobs and Growth launched last spring. Labour leaders have rejected the ideas of fresh talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl to give fresh impulse to the Alliance for Jobs idea, aimed at halving unemployment by the year 2000.

Cologne University Professor Juergen Donges, one of the "Five Wise Men" who advise the German government on economic policy, said the government would have to find new ways to cut spending if it is to meet the convergence criteria.
In a report last November, the panel forecast a 1997 German government budget deficit of 3.3 percent of GDP, above the Maastricht guideline.
"I don't think it is certain that we will fulfill the convergence criteria, but I don't want to exclude it completely," Donges told German radio.

Rexrodt's forecast of driving unemployment back below four million is improbable, as investment remains sluggish, Donges said. "I can seen no quick solution that would lead to a clear retreat in unemployment in 1997, unfortunately," he said.
Ernst Schwanhold, parliamentary finance spokesman for the opposition Social Democrats, said the government's forecast of 2.5 percent growth was unrealistic.
"The government's report contains no conclusive plan to overcome the chronic weakness in investment," Schwanhold said.

The Federation of German Industry (BDI) said the success of government efforts to boost growth, unemployment and investment would depend on whether the business sector got a real boost from planned tax reforms and other policy steps.
Other reforms cited by Rexrodt include pension reform, encouraging venture capital and competition, privatisation of state enterprises and strengthening entrepreneurial companies.
